metaDescription: Six 120V rooftop RV air conditioners from 15,000 to 18,000 BTU compared on heat pump vs electric heat, ducted fit, noise claims and generator demands.
expertTake: The Dometic FreshJet 3 is the best overall pick because it is backwards compatible with the common Dometic ceiling assembly and brings an e-coated evaporator coil to a 15,000 BTU unit. The TURBRO is the value pick for owners who want 1,500W heat and a smart app at a lower tier. Anyone with a 30 amp rig and a small generator should skip the 18,000 BTU units, which ask a lot of both.
introParagraphs: A 120V rooftop air conditioner is the standard way to cool a travel trailer or motorhome. It plugs into the same shore power or generator that runs the rest of the rig, and it moves far more heat than any battery-powered unit can.

The decisions are about capacity, ducting, heating method and what your electrical supply can actually start. A bigger number on the box is only useful if the rig, the roof and the breaker can all carry it.

products.name: Dometic FreshJet 3 Series 15,000 BTU rooftop AC
products.description:
The FreshJet 3 is built around fit and durability. Dometic lists it as backwards compatible with an existing air distribution box, so on a rig that already has a Dometic ceiling assembly, the upgrade is mostly a unit swap. It also uses e-coated evaporator coils, a corrosion treatment the brand says it alone uses among RV air conditioners, which matters on coastal trips and in humid climates where bare aluminum coils pit.

The lighter construction cuts roof load and makes the install a two-person job instead of a three-person one. The tradeoff is that it is a cooling-focused design, so if you want integrated heat you need a different model. It sits in the upper-middle price tier, above the budget RecPro units but below the premium picks. Against the TURBRO, you pay for brand support and coil protection rather than extras like a smart app.

Ownership is helped by the widespread parts and technician familiarity with Dometic. Clean the filter monthly, wash the condenser coil yearly and check the roof gasket each spring. If your rig has a soft-start kit option, fit one, because it is the biggest single lever for running a 15,000 BTU unit on a small generator. Keep the original ceiling assembly photos so a matching swap is easy.
products.bestFor: Owners replacing a Dometic unit who want the easiest swap and coil protection.
pros: Backwards compatible with existing ceiling assembly
cons: Needs a soft start for small generators

products.name: TURBRO 15,000 BTU 115V AC with 1,500W electric heat
products.description:
TURBRO pairs 15,000 BTU of cooling with 1,500 watts of electric heating, a quiet-operation claim as low as 52 dB and control by remote or smart app. The 1,500 watt heater is plain resistance heat, about 12.5 amps at 120 volts, which is simple and works at any temperature but uses more power than a heat pump in mild weather. The ceiling assembly adds an atmosphere lamp and the lift handles make rooftop installation less awkward.

What you give up is brand history and the heat pump efficiency of rivals. The 52 dB figure is a maker claim measured under its own conditions, and rooftop units are usually louder at the ceiling than the number suggests. It lands in the lower-middle price tier, which is its pitch. Compared with the RecPro heat pump models, it heats with more current but is simpler; compared with the Dometic, it adds features but less track record.

Ownership is routine. Clean the filter, wash the coils, check the gasket and keep the app firmware current. With a 1,500W heater, remember that heat mode adds to the electrical load, so do not run it with a microwave on a 30 amp service.
products.bestFor: Cost-conscious owners who want integrated heat and app control.
cons: Noise figure is a maker claim

products.name: RecPro 15K quiet non-ducted heat pump AC, black
products.description:
RecPro markets this non-ducted 15K unit around low amp draw, a built-in heat pump and a 55.4 dB noise rating. A heat pump provides warmth by reversing the refrigeration cycle, so in moderate weather it delivers more heat per watt than a resistance element. The black shell gives a different look from white units, and the UV-resistant plastic is meant to last on a sun-baked roof.

The low amp claim is the useful part for generator owners, since lower running current makes it easier to start on a smaller inverter model, though no unit is exempt from startup surge. The 55.4 dB figure is louder than the TURBRO claim, so light sleepers should weigh it. It sits in the upper tier of the group. Compared with the white ducted RecPro, this version is non-ducted and simpler; against the Dometic, it adds a heat pump.

Ownership centers on keeping the heat pump efficient: clean coils, an unrestricted filter and a tight gasket. Heat pump output drops in near-freezing weather, so keep a supplemental heater for winter trips.
products.bestFor: Generator users who want a heat pump and lower running amps.
cons: 55.4 dB is louder than rivals' claims

products.name: RecPro 15K heat pump AC, ducted or non-ducted, white
products.description:
This white RecPro covers both ducted and non-ducted setups in one model, which is helpful when your rig has ceiling ducts or you are unsure which ceiling assembly you will need. It shares the 15,000 BTU cooling and built-in heat pump of the black version, along with the low amp draw marketing and a 55.4 dB rating.

The flexibility is the point. A ducted install sends air through ceiling plenums to multiple vents, which spreads cooling more evenly in a long trailer than a single non-ducted outlet. The cost is that ducting depends on the ceiling assembly kit you choose, so verify compatibility before ordering. It sits in the middle of the price range.

Ownership requires attention to duct cleanliness and seals, since leaky ducts lose cooled air into the ceiling cavity. Clean filters, coils and gaskets on schedule, and keep supplemental heat for freezing weather.
products.bestFor: Rigs with ceiling ducts or owners who want install flexibility.

products.name: Arsenda 18,000 BTU 110-120V non-ducted heat pump AC
products.description:
The Arsenda is the high-capacity option at 18,000 BTU with a heat pump and R32 refrigerant, which the listing says gives faster cooling. Extra capacity helps in big rigs, in direct sun or in hot climates where a 15,000 BTU unit runs flat out all afternoon.

The cautions are electrical. An 18,000 BTU compressor pulls more running current and a bigger startup surge, so it asks more from a 30 amp pedestal and much more from a small generator. The listing also notes it needs both 115V AC and 12V DC connections, so verify your rig has a clean 12V feed at the roof. It lands in the lowest price tier of the group.

Ownership requires clean coils, a good gasket and a soft-start accessory if running on a generator. Do not run it alongside a second large appliance on a 30 amp service.
products.bestFor: Large rigs in hot climates with strong shore power.

products.name: LAOFINA 18,000 BTU 110-120V non-ducted heat pump AC
products.description:
LAOFINA offers 18,000 BTU with a heat pump and a 50 dB noise claim, the lowest noise figure among the 120V units here. The listing states plainly that both 115V AC and 12V DC connections are required, which is a useful honest note for installers.

It shares the Arsenda's electrical demands: bigger compressor, bigger surge, and a need for a stout power source. The noise claim is a maker number, not a measurement. The price tier is second lowest of the group. Against the Arsenda, it competes on the noise claim rather than refrigerant details.

Ownership follows the usual pattern: filter, coils, gasket and a soft start for generator use. Confirm that the roof opening and ceiling assembly match before ordering. Photograph the install for any warranty claim.
products.bestFor: Quiet-minded owners with strong power in hot climates.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A 15,000 BTU unit draws roughly 13 to 16 amps running, and its start surge can be several times that without a soft start. On a 30 amp service, one air conditioner plus modest loads is the practical ceiling. Check your inverter generator's surge rating before choosing 18,000 BTU units like the Arsenda or LAOFINA. The common mistake is checking the running amps on the label and forgetting that the first second of compressor start can pull several times that number.

A 15,000 BTU unit handles roughly 700 square feet and under. The 18,000 BTU models suit larger or sun-baked rigs, but oversizing causes short cycling and uneven humidity. Match capacity to length, windows and climate. Short cycling leaves a damp, clammy cabin because the evaporator never runs long enough to wring out humidity.

The RecPro and Arsenda use heat pumps, while the TURBRO adds a 1,500W resistance element. Heat pumps are efficient in mild weather but lose output near freezing. Resistance heat works anywhere but draws about 12.5 amps. If your nights drop below about 40 degrees, plan a propane furnace as the primary heat source regardless of which unit you buy.

A ducted unit sends air through ceiling plenums to several vents, while a non-ducted unit blows from one ceiling assembly. The white RecPro handles both. Replacing a ducted system with a non-ducted one changes the ceiling hardware. Check the ceiling assembly in your rig before ordering, because the mismatch is the most common return reason.

The LAOFINA claims 50 dB, TURBRO 52 dB and RecPro 55.4 dB. These are maker figures, and ceiling placement makes them louder. A few decibels is audible when you try to sleep. Rubber isolation pads under the unit help, but the biggest noise fix is a tight roof mount.

The Dometic FreshJet 3 is backwards compatible with existing assemblies and has e-coated coils. Others use a standard roof opening. Coastal and humid climates favor coil protection. Roof opening is 14 inches square on most rigs, but ceiling thickness varies and affects the gasket.

howWeEvaluated.title: Electrical demand
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered running and starting load, since generator compatibility is the main limiter. 18,000 BTU units ranked lower for small power systems. We assumed a typical 30 amp trailer, since that is the most common setup, and flagged anything that strains it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Heating design
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared heat pumps with the TURBRO's 1,500W element. Heat pumps scored higher for efficiency, while resistance heat scored higher for cold-weather reliability.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit and compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: The Dometic's backwards compatibility and RecPro's ducted option counted. Installation friction decides satisfaction, so units that match existing hardware were rewarded.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise claims
howWeEvaluated.description: We recorded 50 to 55.4 dB claims and treated them as best case.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value across tiers
howWeEvaluated.description: We judged what each tier buys, from Arsenda at the lowest to RecPro at the top. We also noted that two 18,000 BTU units share nearly identical specifications, so the ranking reflects listing clarity.

maintenance.why: Dust restricts airflow and can freeze the coil. Rinse the foam in warm water and dry fully before refitting. A fresh filter also keeps the heat pump efficient.
Dirty coils raise head pressure and power use. Use a soft brush and a gentle hose, never a pressure washer, which bends fins.
A worn gasket leaks into the ceiling.
Weak start capacitors cause hard starts. A weak capacitor shows up as slow starting or humming. A technician can test it in minutes.
Loose power terminals heat under load.

faq.q: Can I run a 15,000 BTU unit on a 30 amp service?
faq.a: Yes, with care. Avoid running it together with a microwave or water heater element. Running the AC alone on a 30 amp circuit leaves room for a fridge and a few lights.

faq.q: Do I need a soft start?
faq.a: For small generators, yes. It sharply reduces the starting surge. Many owners report that adding a soft start lets a smaller inverter generator start the unit.
Tiers run from Arsenda at the low end to Dometic and RecPro at the top. Prices change, so check listings.
Heat pump for mild weather, resistance for cold.
For most trailers, yes. They suit large rigs in hot climates. Oversized units also cost more to run and may short cycle.

faq.q: Can I swap ducted for non-ducted?
faq.a: Only by changing the ceiling assembly.
